title: A/B Testing Emails: What to Test and How to Measure Results

facts.fact: The page states that email open rates in email marketing can hover anywhere from 20-30%, a range it presents without citing a source.
facts.quote: In email marketing, where open rates can hover anywhere from **20-30%**, even a tiny improvement can have an outsized impact as your list grows.

facts.fact: In a test the page describes, a brand sent two subject lines to 4,000 subscribers, and the subject line "[Sale] Get Our Products For 50% Off" reached a 13.25% open rate.
facts.quote: I saw a test once where a brand sent two subject lines to a group of **4,000** subscribers. The first, **"[Sale] Get Our Products For 50% Off"**, hit a **13.25% open rate**.

facts.fact: In the same described test of 4,000 subscribers, the subject line "Sale: Get Our Products For 50% Off" reached a 12.5% open rate.
facts.quote: The second, **"Sale: Get Our Products For 50% Off"**, only got a **12.5% open rate**.

facts.fact: The page reports that in the described subject-line test, using brackets instead of a colon produced a 0.75% uplift.
facts.quote: That tiny change (using brackets instead of a colon) created a **0.75%** uplift.

facts.fact: The page defines a valid email A/B test as one where Version A (control) and Version B (variation) differ in only one element.
facts.quote: You create two versions of your email, **Version A** (the control) and **Version B** (the variation), with only **one difference** between them.

facts.fact: The page recommends sending each A/B test version to a small, random slice of the email list before sending the winner to the rest of the audience.
facts.quote: You send each version to a small, random slice of your email list.
